analysis.one_liner: Gives every child a $1,000 government savings account at birth with yearly deposits for lower-income families.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal savings account for every child, seeded with $1,000 at birth. Each year until the child turned 18, the government would add more — up to $2,000 a year for the poorest families, tapering off as family income rises. At 18, the child could spend the money on college or job training, a first home, or leave it invested until later in life. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never went anywhere: no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every child born after 2023 would get a savings account worth at least $1,000 at birth, growing to several thousand dollars or more with interest by age 18. Lower-income families get the largest annual deposits, and the account would not reduce their eligibility for other federal benefits. Children of wealthy families (above 500% of poverty line income) get the $1,000 seed but no yearly additions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children of low- and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 2023 would receive a $1,000 federal savings account at birth.
Annual contributions of up to $2,000 per year are targeted to lower- and middle-income families, scaling down on a sliding scale and phasing out above 500 percent of the poverty line.
Account balances, including investment earnings, would be tax-exempt, and the balances would not count against eligibility for federal benefits such as student financial aid.
Money could be used for education, a first home, or long-term investment after age 18, and unlike 529-style plans, requires no family money up front.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through general Treasury revenues, since the bill bars using payroll taxes and funds accounts directly from the general fund; no single industry bears a direct cost, though the investment would be limited to government bonds rather than private financial products.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates an expensive open-ended entitlement: every child born after 2023 gets $1,000 at birth, with annual payments up to $2,000 per child, all drawn from the Treasury's general fund — a substantial long-term federal outlay.
Money is locked up for 18 years and can only be spent on the allowed purposes before age 59½, so it is less flexible than giving families the same money as cash now.
Funds are invested only in government securities, so families forgo potentially higher market returns in exchange for safety.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits for low-income children are large and long-term, but the bill's costs to taxpayers over an 18-year horizon are also large, and money locked away in a federal fund cannot be used for other needs like health coverage or direct cash assistance today. The design — income-graded contributions, no benefit cliffs, broad qualified uses — is unusually well done for a wealth-building bill, so the main objection is cost and priorities rather than design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee two weeks after it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year congressional session ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 14, 2023, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
That was the only action ever taken on it: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the entire two-year Congress.
It gathered 33 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and no Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No public program was created, so taxpayers avoided a long-term cost, and the existing college-savings industry kept its market. Children born without family wealth got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers avoided the cost; existing savings industry kept its market

industries.note: They pay for the program through general federal revenues but receive no contributions for their own children. The largest standing cost falls on federal taxpayers overall.

industries.industry: Private 529 plan managers and financial services firms
industries.note: A universal public savings program run by a federal board competes with private college-savings products and keeps these accounts out of fee-charging private funds.
